vignette:
Marcus

Marcus sits in the leather chair with his shoulders drawn inward, his dark eyes fixed on a point somewhere beyond the office window. At twenty-two, he carries himself with an unusual formality—the kind of careful composure that suggests someone perpetually braced for criticism. He is the principal of a mid-sized secondary school, a position that seems incongruous with his age until he begins to explain how he arrived there.

He grew up in Lagos with his father, a man whose own childhood had been marked by deprivation and who believed that discipline—harsh, unrelenting discipline—was the only language children truly understood. Marcus's earliest memories are not of play or laughter but of waiting. Waiting to hear his father's footsteps on the stairs. Waiting to know what infraction he had committed without realizing it. The beatings were frequent and severe. His father used his belt, his hands, whatever was nearest. Marcus learned to move quietly, to keep his grades perfect, to anticipate needs before they were expressed. He learned that love and fear were the same thing.

When Marcus was sixteen, his father died suddenly of a heart attack. Within a year, Marcus had thrown himself into academics with an intensity that alarmed his teachers. He moved through secondary school and into university with single-minded determination, eventually securing a position as principal through a combination of genuine competence and something else—a desperate need to prove his worth, to establish control in at least one domain of his life.

The job suits him in some ways. He is excellent with structure, with discipline, with creating order. But it has also become a mirror he cannot escape. When a student makes a mistake, Marcus feels his chest tighten. When a teacher questions his decision, something primal awakens in him—a child's panic at the prospect of punishment. He finds himself raising his voice in ways that surprise him, then spending hours afterward consumed with shame and self-recrimination.

His relationship with his girlfriend, Zainab, has become increasingly strained. She notices that he cannot accept comfort. When she reaches for him at night, he sometimes flinches, even though he knows it is her. He has told her nothing about his father, offering only vague references to a "difficult childhood," and he experiences her attempts at closeness as somehow threatening—as though tenderness is a luxury he does not deserve and cannot trust. He finds himself picking fights over small things, then withdrawing into an impenetrable silence that can last for days.

At night, Marcus does not sleep well. He dreams of his father's shadow in the doorway, of the sound of the belt being unbuckled, of his own small voice asking what he did wrong. He wakes with his heart racing, drenched in sweat, and lies in the darkness trying to convince himself that he is safe. By morning, he feels hollowed out, moving through his day as though watching himself from outside his body.

He has started having intrusive thoughts at work—sudden, vivid memories of specific beatings that pull him away from conversations mid-sentence. He finds himself scanning rooms for exits, for potential threats. He drinks more than he used to, telling himself it helps him sleep, though it rarely does. He has begun to wonder if he is fundamentally broken, if the damage his father inflicted is simply too deep to repair, if he is destined to carry this weight alone forever.
